Q: When is a fixed workflow better than an autonomous agent?
A:
**Delegation splits a task across workers; it does not split accountability automatically.** Use multiple agents when independent capabilities or parallel investigations justify the coordination cost. A supervisor selects work, workers produce bounded artifacts, and a coordinator validates and merges them under one task contract. Several copies of the same model can share the same blind spot; agreement is not independent factual evidence.

Define ownership of state, budgets, cancellation and effects before parallelizing. Read-only workers can return source-linked findings, but one authoritative executor should control a shared irreversible operation. Pass only the minimum permitted context to each worker and bind delegated identity/scope explicitly. A worker must not inherit all supervisor privileges merely because it received a task.

Suppose two specialists both recommend creating the same support ticket. If each creates its own operation ID, the provider can legitimately create two tickets despite per-key deduplication. The coordinator must identify the single logical business effect and serialize its approval/execution. The support fixture races two workers on one stable operation to expose that invariant; it does not claim model collaboration quality or distributed consensus.

Parallelism can reduce wall time for independent calls but raises total token/tool cost and can overload a shared dependency. Reserve a shared budget, cap concurrency and choose a failure policy: cancel all on critical missing evidence, return a labeled partial result, or retry only the failed independent step. Persist accepted artifacts and schema versions so restart does not rerun every worker or duplicate writes. Compare against a single workflow using the same task suite and effect oracle; if delegation adds no measured benefit, keep the simpler design.
Why: Two specialists independently propose the same ticket. Stable business identity and one approved executor prevent duplicate effects; two fresh random operation IDs would defeat the intended deduplication.
Risk: Delegated context can disclose private evidence to a less trusted worker. Parallel agreement can amplify a shared hallucination rather than validate a claim.
Trade: Specialization and parallel reads can help complex tasks, but increase coordination, cost and debugging. A single explicit workflow is often easier to bound and recover.
Try: Use the support race test to model two workers requesting one effect. Then design a two-read-worker budget and compare total attempts and latency assumptions against a sequential baseline.

follow_ups.Q: What if one worker fails after the other has committed an effect?
follow_ups.A: Stop treating the run as an all-or-nothing computation. Reconcile the committed operation, preserve its audit and decide whether to continue or perform an explicitly authorized compensation; restarting every worker with fresh keys is unsafe.

Q: How should orchestration state be modeled?
A: Represent goal, principal reference, completed steps, pending actions, evidence IDs, budget, and terminal status explicitly. Keep durable operation outcomes separate from model-generated plans.
Why: Use typed transitions and immutable identifiers. Persist checkpoints at recoverable boundaries and validate loaded state before resuming.
Risk: A checkpoint can be stale relative to the business database.
Trade: Explicit state adds modeling work and makes restart behavior understandable.
Try: Resume after a crash between a completed tool call and the next model call.

Q: What is fan-out and fan-in orchestration?
A: Fan-out runs independent tasks concurrently; fan-in combines their results under a declared policy. Parallel execution is useful only when tasks do not require each other's outputs.
Why: Bound concurrency and define whether aggregation requires all results, a quorum, or best-effort partial output. Preserve per-branch errors and provenance.
Risk: One slow branch can delay completion or cause unbounded task growth.
Trade: Parallelism reduces latency and raises peak load and coordination cost.
Try: Search three authorized corpora concurrently and report one failed branch without hiding it.

A: Use a directed dependency graph when tasks require earlier outputs. Validate that the graph is acyclic unless a bounded loop has deliberate semantics.
Why: Execute ready nodes, propagate typed outputs, and make failure handling explicit per edge. A task plan does not establish permission.
Risk: Incorrect dependency declarations can execute a write before validation.
Trade: Graphs improve visibility while increasing orchestration machinery.
Try: Model extract, validate, review, and submit with a required approval edge.

Q: How does durable execution differ from retrying the whole agent?
A: Durable execution resumes from recorded progress instead of blindly repeating every prior action. It requires deliberate handling of nondeterministic work and external side effects.
Why: Persist operation keys and results, and make repeated execution safe at each resumable boundary. Checkpoint behavior depends on the runtime and version.
Risk: Replaying a node can duplicate a write if the business operation is not idempotent.
Trade: Durability adds storage and state evolution work.
Try: Demonstrate a crash after external execution but before checkpoint persistence.

Q: What should an orchestrator do when one tool fails?
A: Classify failure by cause and effect: invalid input, denied access, transient outage, uncertain completion, or terminal business rejection. Select retry, clarification, status lookup, fallback, or escalation accordingly.
Why: Apply a remaining-deadline budget and preserve the original operation ID across uncertain retries.
Risk: Treating every exception as retryable can multiply writes or provider load.
Trade: Detailed policies require maintenance and avoid broad unsafe retries.
Try: Write a failure table with an allowed recovery action for each category.

Q: How should human approval be represented in a workflow?
A: Approval is a server-verified event bound to a specific principal, operation, parameters, expiry, and revision. A waiting workflow state should reference that approval requirement.
Why: Resume only after checking the approval and current business state. Reject stale approvals after material parameter changes.
Risk: A graph interrupt or chat message is not an authorization proof.
Trade: Explicit approvals add latency and auditability.
Try: Modify an approved operation and verify that the workflow returns to review.

Q: How should shared memory work across multiple agents?
A: Share only scoped facts and artifacts that each participant needs. Use a coordinator-owned task record and explicit output contracts instead of a writable universal scratchpad.
Why: Track who produced each fact and which service can verify it. Merge conflicts through rules rather than last-writer-wins prose.
Risk: One agent's unsupported assumption can spread to all others.
Trade: Restricted sharing reduces context reuse and limits error propagation.
Try: Have two agents disagree on a version and require evidence-based reconciliation.

Q: How do you prevent orchestration cost explosions?
A: Bound total model calls, tool calls, elapsed time, parallel tasks, and spend per user task. Include retries and critic loops in the same budget.
Why: Stop at an explicit terminal state and explain incomplete work using recorded outcomes. Apply fleet-level quotas in addition to local semaphores.
Risk: Nested agents can each obey a local limit while exceeding the parent task budget.
Trade: Tight budgets reduce task coverage and control operational risk.
Try: Build a parent budget that every child operation must reserve before execution.

Why: Use deterministic replay where possible, sandbox external effects, and inject crashes at durable boundaries.
Risk: Matching one reference sequence can reject alternative valid solutions.
Trade: Invariant-based evaluation accepts valid diversity and requires thoughtful specifications.
